Protactinium
Kasimir Fajans, Oswald Göhring; Lise Meitner and Otto Hahn
Germany
From the Greek protos, «first»: when it decays it forms actinium.
Fajans and Göhring found a very short-lived isotope in 1913. In 1917-18 Meitner and Hahn found the longest-lived isotope, protactinium-231.
It is one of the rarest natural elements; it occurs in traces in uranium ores.
Research only, for example for dating ocean sediments.
In 1961 the United Kingdom produced about 125 grams of it by processing 60 tonnes of nuclear waste: almost all that exists.
Uranium
Martin Heinrich Klaproth
Germany
From the planet Uranus, discovered a few years earlier (1781).
Klaproth found it in 1789 in pitchblende. In 1896 Becquerel discovered radioactivity thanks to a uranium salt forgotten on a photographic plate.
It occurs in many rocks; it is mined mostly in Kazakhstan, Canada and Australia.
Fuel for nuclear power plants, submarine propulsion, dating rocks; it once coloured glass yellow-green.
One kilogram of uranium-235 can produce as much energy as almost 3,000 tonnes of coal. Uranium glass glows green under UV light.
Neptunium
Edwin McMillan, Philip Abelson
United States
From the planet Neptune, which comes after Uranus.
It was the first transuranium element, made in 1940 at Berkeley by bombarding uranium with neutrons. Fermi in Rome had come close as early as 1934.
Traces form in uranium ores; it is produced in nuclear reactors.
Making plutonium-238 for space batteries, neutron detectors.
Uranium, neptunium and plutonium follow the order of the planets: Uranus, Neptune, Pluto.
Plutonium
Glenn Seaborg, Edwin McMillan, Joseph Kennedy, Arthur Wahl
United States
From Pluto, then considered the planet after Neptune.
It was produced at Berkeley at the end of 1940 by bombarding uranium with deuterons. The discovery remained secret until the end of the war.
It is produced in nuclear reactors; minute traces exist in nature.
Nuclear fuel (MOX), radioisotope batteries for space probes (plutonium-238), nuclear weapons.
The Voyager probes, now beyond the Solar System, are powered by the heat of plutonium-238.
Americium
Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James, Leon Morgan, Albert Ghiorso
United States
From America, just as europium comes from Europe.
It was produced in 1944 in Chicago during the Manhattan Project. Seaborg announced the discovery on a children's radio quiz show, before the official conference!
It is produced in nuclear reactors.
Household smoke detectors (americium-241), industrial gauges.
You probably have a tiny bit of americium at home: inside many smoke detectors.
Curium
Glenn Seaborg, Ralph James, Albert Ghiorso
United States
In honour of Marie and Pierre Curie.
It was produced in 1944 at Berkeley by bombarding plutonium with alpha particles.
It is produced in nuclear reactors.
Alpha X-ray spectrometers on Mars rovers, power sources for probes.
The Curiosity rover analyses Martian rocks with an instrument that uses curium.
Berkelium
Stanley Thompson, Albert Ghiorso, Glenn Seaborg
United States
From the city of Berkeley, in California.
It was produced in December 1949 by bombarding americium with alpha particles.
It is produced in milligram amounts in a few special reactors.
Target for making heavier elements, such as tennessine.
Less than 2 grams of it have been produced in all of history.
Californium
Stanley Thompson, Kenneth Street, Albert Ghiorso, Glenn Seaborg
United States
From California.
It was produced in 1950 at Berkeley by bombarding curium with alpha particles.
It is produced in tiny amounts in special reactors.
Neutron sources to start reactors, search for gold and oil, detect explosives, treat tumours.
A single gram of californium-252 emits more than 2 billion neutrons per second.
Einsteinium
Albert Ghiorso and co-workers
United States
In honour of Albert Einstein.
It was found in 1952 in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb, «Ivy Mike», in the Pacific. The discovery was kept secret until 1955.
Invisible amounts are produced in high-flux reactors.
Scientific research only.
It was discovered by analysing dust collected by planes flying through the mushroom cloud.
Fermium
Albert Ghiorso and co-workers
United States
In honour of Enrico Fermi, the physicist from Rome.
It was found together with einsteinium in the debris of the 1952 «Ivy Mike» explosion.
It is produced only in laboratories, in infinitesimal amounts.
Scientific research only.
It is the heaviest element that can be made by bombarding with neutrons: going further requires accelerators.
Mendelevium
Albert Ghiorso, Glenn Seaborg, Bernard Harvey, Gregory Choppin, Stanley Thompson
United States
In honour of Dmitri Mendeleev, the father of the periodic table.
It was created in 1955 at Berkeley by bombarding einsteinium: at first they obtained just 17 atoms in total.
It is produced only in laboratories, one atom at a time.
Scientific research only.
It was the first element discovered one atom at a time.
Nobelium
Dubna Institute (Georgy Flerov and co-workers)
Russia (USSR)
In honour of Alfred Nobel.
A team in Stockholm announced its discovery in 1957, but it was wrong. The definite proof came from the Dubna laboratory in 1966; the Swedish name was kept anyway.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
It is named after the inventor of dynamite and of the Nobel Prizes.
Lawrencium
Albert Ghiorso, Torbjørn Sikkeland, Almon Larsh, Robert Latimer
United States
In honour of Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron.
It was produced in 1961 at Berkeley by bombarding californium with boron ions.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
It closes the actinide series.
Rutherfordium
Dubna (USSR) and Berkeley (USA)
Russia / United States
In honour of Ernest Rutherford, who discovered the atomic nucleus.
Soviet and American laboratories both claimed its discovery (1964 and 1969) during the so-called «Transfermium Wars». The name was settled only in 1997.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
For years it had two names: kurchatovium for the Russians and rutherfordium for the Americans.
Dubnium
Dubna (USSR) and Berkeley (USA)
Russia / United States
From the city of Dubna, home of the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research.
It was claimed by Dubna in 1968 and by Berkeley in 1970; the credit was later shared.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
It is one of the few elements named after a Russian city.
Seaborgium
Albert Ghiorso and co-workers
United States
In honour of Glenn Seaborg.
It was produced in 1974 at Berkeley by bombarding californium with oxygen.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
It was the first element named after a living person: Seaborg could write his address using element names.
Bohrium
Peter Armbruster, Gottfried Münzenberg (GSI)
Germany
In honour of Niels Bohr.
It was created in 1981 at the GSI in Darmstadt by bombarding bismuth with chromium.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
It is named after the scientist who drew the atom with electrons in orbits, like the one you see in this app.
Hassium
Peter Armbruster, Gottfried Münzenberg (GSI)
Germany
From Hassia, the Latin name of Hesse, the German region of Darmstadt.
It was created in 1984 at the GSI by bombarding lead with iron.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
It is the heaviest element whose chemistry has been studied: it forms an oxide like osmium.
Meitnerium
Peter Armbruster, Gottfried Münzenberg (GSI)
Germany
In honour of Lise Meitner, who explained nuclear fission.
It was created in 1982 at the GSI: the discovery was based on a single atom.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
Lise Meitner did not receive the Nobel Prize for fission, but she has an element of her own: a rarer honour.
Darmstadtium
Sigurd Hofmann and co-workers (GSI)
Germany
From the city of Darmstadt.
It was created in 1994 at the GSI by bombarding lead with nickel.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
Only a few dozen atoms have ever been created.
Roentgenium
Sigurd Hofmann and co-workers (GSI)
Germany
In honour of Wilhelm Röntgen, discoverer of X-rays.
It was created in 1994 at the GSI by bombarding bismuth with nickel.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
It sits below gold in the table: chemists think it would be an even «nobler» noble metal.
Copernicium
Sigurd Hofmann and co-workers (GSI)
Germany
In honour of Nicolaus Copernicus.
It was created in 1996 at the GSI by bombarding lead with zinc.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
Its name was announced on 19 February 2010, Copernicus's birthday.
Nihonium
Kosuke Morita and co-workers (RIKEN)
Japan
From Nihon, «Japan» in Japanese.
RIKEN created it in 2004 by bombarding bismuth with zinc; confirming it took 9 years of experiments and just 3 atoms.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
It is the first element discovered in Asia.
Flerovium
Yuri Oganessian and co-workers (Dubna)
Russia
In honour of Georgy Flerov, founder of the Dubna laboratory.
It was created at Dubna in 1998-99 by bombarding plutonium with calcium-48.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
Some scientists think it might behave almost like a noble gas.
Moscovium
Dubna and Lawrence Livermore
Russia / United States
From the Moscow region.
It was created in 2003 at Dubna by bombarding americium with calcium-48.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
Before it had an official name it was called «ununpentium», meaning «one-one-five» in Latin.
Livermorium
Dubna and Lawrence Livermore
Russia / United States
From the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California.
It was created at Dubna in 2000 by bombarding curium with calcium-48.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
Each atom created lives only a few milliseconds.
Tennessine
Dubna, Oak Ridge, Vanderbilt
Russia / United States
From the US state of Tennessee.
It was created in 2010 at Dubna by bombarding berkelium, made specially at Oak Ridge, with calcium-48.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
To create it, berkelium had to be flown from the USA to Russia in a hurry, because it decays.
Oganesson
Yuri Oganessian and co-workers (Dubna, Livermore)
Russia / United States
In honour of the physicist Yuri Oganessian.
It was created in 2002 at Dubna by bombarding californium with calcium-48; only about 5 atoms have been observed so far.
It is produced only in accelerators.
Scientific research only.
It is the heaviest element ever created. It is the second element named after a living person, after seaborgium.
